On 29 June 2013 Mr Starov, Ms Pitenova, Mr Fedorov and Mr Prokopenko took part in a demonstration involving about eighty participants in St Petersburg aimed at drawing attention to violations of the rights of LGBTI people in Russia.
On 12 October 2013 Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina intended to take part in a demonstration in St Petersburg to mark Coming Out Day.

Some applicants complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully during peaceful demonstrations in support of LGBTI people.

At 1.55 p.m. on 12 October 2013, five minutes before the demonstration started, the police began apprehending the participants, including Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina, on the grounds that they had used foul language.
At 2.30 p.m. on 12 October 2013 the police escorted Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina to a police station.

Administrative-offence reports were drawn up against Mr Fedorov, Mr Prokopenko and Ms Levina under Article 20.1 § 1 ('petty hooliganism' – мелкое хулиганство) of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation following their apprehension on 12 October 2013.
The administrative-offence report in respect of Mr Fedorov was drawn up at 7.50 p.m. on 12 October 2013 and he was released at 8 p.m.
The administrative-offence report in respect of Mr Prokopenko was drawn up at 4.05 p.m. on 12 October 2013 and he was released at 7.05 p.m.
The administrative-offence report in respect of Ms Levina was drawn up at 5.25 p.m. on 12 October 2013 and she was released at 6.50 p.m.
Mr Fedorov and Ms Levina complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully, before the start of the authorised demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.
On 26 February 2015 the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed the complaint by Mr Fedorov and Ms Levina that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully on 12 October 2013.
On 29 April 2016 the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation finally upheld the Kuybyshevskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision dismissing the complaint by Mr Fedorov and Ms Levina.

Mr Prokopenko brought a civil action seeking compensation for non-pecuniary damage caused by his being unlawfully apprehended and detained before the start of the authorised demonstration of 12 October 2013 in St Petersburg.

On 10 February 2015 the Petrogradskiy District Court of St Petersburg awarded Mr Prokopenko 2,000 Russian roubles (RUB), equivalent to approximately 27 euros (EUR), in respect of non-pecuniary damage for his unlawful apprehension and detention on 12 October 2013.
On 9 June 2015 the St Petersburg City Court dismissed an appeal by Mr Prokopenko against the Petrogradskiy District Court's award of 2,000 RUB in non-pecuniary damages.
On 1 December 2015 a judge of the St Petersburg City Court refused to refer a cassation appeal lodged by Mr Prokopenko to the Presidium of that court for examination.
On 6 March 2014 the St Petersburg City Court discontinued the administrative-offence proceedings against Mr Prokopenko for lack of evidence.

Mr Chechetkin was nearby when the two intruders were stopped in the corridor of the HIV prevention centre on 3 November 2013.

The police arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.
An ambulance arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.

All persons questioned by the police between November 2013 and February 2014 about the attack of 3 November 2013 alleged that the attack had been motivated by hatred against LGBTI people.

Ms P. noted that on the day of the attack on 3 November 2013 a social network community called 'Wolf-Homophobe' ('Волк-Гомофоб') had published a post about the upcoming attack in St Petersburg on its webpage.
The investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin identified and questioned several people who had participated in actions against the LGBTI community.
None of the fingerprints of the people questioned by the investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin matched those found at the scene of the attack on 3 November 2013.

While firing at Mr Romanov, Mr L. shouted 'sodomy is a mortal sin'.

In his statement of 17 May 2012, Mr L. explained that he had come to the 'Rainbow flash mob' event to 'fight sexual minorities'.
On 17 February 2013 an investigator questioned Mr L.

One of the aims of the 'Sin-free City' movement was to fight the 'propaganda of perversion', including homosexuality.
On 17 July 2013 Mr Romanov requested the investigator to explore alleged motives of hate against LGBTI people in the case concerning the attack on him on 17 May 2012.
By a decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator dismissed Mr Romanov's request to explore hate motives against LGBTI people for 'lack of any evidence of hate motives'.

In the decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator indicated that Mr L. had not insulted anyone, had come to the event by accident, and that his actions had been motivated by the blasphemous words on the balloon.

The Petrogradskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced Mr L. to one year's imprisonment, conditional on one year's probation.
On 18 December 2013 the State Duma of the Russian Federation amnestied Mr L.

On 10 February 2015 the Petrogradskiy District Court of St Petersburg awarded Mr Prokopenko 2,000 Russian roubles (RUB), equivalent to approximately 27 euros (EUR), in respect of non-pecuniary damage for his unlawful apprehension and detention on 12 October 2013.
On 9 June 2015 the St Petersburg City Court dismissed an appeal by Mr Prokopenko against the Petrogradskiy District Court's award of 2,000 RUB in non-pecuniary damages.
On 1 December 2015 a judge of the St Petersburg City Court refused to refer a cassation appeal lodged by Mr Prokopenko to the Presidium of that court for examination.
On 3 November 2013 Mr Chechetkin attended the 'Rainbow Tea Social', a weekly event held to support LGBTI people, at an HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg.

At around 7.15 p.m. on 3 November 2013 two young men in hoods armed with a baseball bat and an air gun entered the HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg where the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event was being held.
The two intruders were stopped in the corridor of the HIV prevention centre by Ms P., one of the organisers of the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event.
Mr Chechetkin was nearby when the two intruders were stopped in the corridor of the HIV prevention centre on 3 November 2013.
As soon as Mr Chechetkin turned his head in the direction of the intruders, one of them shot him in the left eye with an air gun.
After being shot in the left eye, Mr Chechetkin crouched down and tried to hide.
One of the attackers shouted 'where are you going, faggot?' at Mr Chechetkin and then approached him and hit him in the shoulder and leg with a baseball bat.
After attacking Mr Chechetkin, the two men left the HIV prevention centre.
The police arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.
An ambulance arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.
The police found and collected evidence at the HIV prevention centre following the attack on 3 November 2013, including three metal bullets, several shoe prints, palm prints and fingerprints.
After the attack on 3 November 2013, Mr Chechetkin underwent surgery on his eye.
The pellet was removed from Mr Chechetkin's eye following surgery, but he lost sight in his left eye.
On 4 November 2013, at the request of Ms P., the police opened a criminal case in respect of the attack on Mr Chechetkin at the HIV prevention centre.
The attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013 was classified under Article 213 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as a disorderly act committed by a group.
Between November 2013 and February 2014 the police questioned Mr Chechetkin, Ms P. and more than fifteen other participants in the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event about the attack of 3 November 2013.
All persons questioned by the police between November 2013 and February 2014 about the attack of 3 November 2013 alleged that the attack had been motivated by hatred against LGBTI people.

Ms P. noted that on the day of the attack on 3 November 2013 a social network community called 'Wolf-Homophobe' ('Волк-Гомофоб') had published a post about the upcoming attack in St Petersburg on its webpage.
The investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin identified and questioned several people who had participated in actions against the LGBTI community.
None of the fingerprints of the people questioned by the investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin matched those found at the scene of the attack on 3 November 2013.

On 24 December 2013 the investigator refused an application by Mr Chechetkin's lawyer for the perpetrators' actions to be classified under Article 111 § 3 (a) and (b) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as actions committed by a group of persons for motives of hatred or enmity towards LGBTI people.

On 5 March 2014 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed an appeal against the investigator's decision of 24 December 2013 refusing to classify the perpetrators' actions as motivated by hatred or enmity towards LGBTI people, holding that it was premature to decide on the legal classification of the offence at such an early stage of the proceedings.

On 21 April 2014 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 5 March 2014 dismissing the appeal against the investigator's refusal to reclassify the offence.
On 16 July 2014 the investigator suspended the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin on the grounds that the attackers could not be identified.
On 6 March 2015 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed an appeal by Mr Chechetkin against the investigator's decision of 16 July 2014 to suspend the investigation.
On 6 March 2015 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed a further application by Mr Chechetkin to have the perpetrators' actions classified as motivated by hatred.
On 7 May 2015 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 6 March 2015.
The investigators suspended and resumed the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin multiple times, most recently on 7 October 2017, without achieving any tangible results.
Mr Chechetkin has not received any further information about the progress of the investigation into the attack on him since 7 October 2017.
On 14 October 2017 Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin were in a bar in St Petersburg.
At around 5 p.m. on 14 October 2017 a man unknown to Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin noticed a rainbow bracelet on their friend's hand and approached them.
The man who approached Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017 insulted them while referring to their perceived homosexuality.
The man who approached Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017 beat them, inflicting several bruises which were recorded by a doctor later that day.
On 15 October 2017 Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin reported the incident of 14 October 2017 to the police.

On 23 October 2017 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, stating that 'the attack had amounted to an administrative offence under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation' ('battery').

On 15 February 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 23 October 2017 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered the police to carry out additional inquiries, notably to obtain video-recordings from webcams, identify and question witnesses and obtain the opinion of a medical expert.

On 3 March 2018 the police opened administrative-offence proceedings under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin.

On 19 March 2018 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, essentially reiterating the reasons given in their first refusal of 23 October 2017.

On 12 July 2018 the police refused to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin, essentially reiterating the reasons given in their first refusal of 23 October 2017.
On 29 May 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 19 March 2018 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered additional inquiries.
On 28 December 2018 a prosecutor quashed the police's decision of 12 July 2018 refusing to institute criminal proceedings and ordered additional inquiries.
No criminal investigation was ever instituted in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on 14 October 2017.
On 19 December 2018 the applicants' lawyer challenged the police's decision of 12 July 2018 refusing to institute criminal proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin.

On 15 January 2019 the Nevskiy District Court of St Petersburg discontinued the proceedings challenging the police's decision of 12 July 2018 on the basis that the impugned decision had already been quashed.
On 24 April 2019 the St Petersburg City Court endorsed the Nevskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 15 January 2019.
On 14 October 2019 the police discontinued the administrative proceedings in relation to the attack on Ms Gromadskaya and Mr Martin on the grounds that the limitation period had expired.
